title: A hidden ocean change near Antarctica could have global consequences
gist: A new study finds Antarctic Intermediate Water, a 2,300-4,000 ft layer circling Antarctica, has turned saltier since 2016 sea-ice losses, reversing decades of freshening, with possible global effects on heat, carbon and weather within years.

insights.claim: Researchers documented a sharp salinity increase in the Southern Ocean's Antarctic Intermediate Water at 2,300 to 4,000 feet depth, reversing decades of freshening, using six datasets (2004-2024) including Argo floats.
insights.speaker: Inside Climate News
insights.so_what: A rapid regime change in a climate-critical layer.

insights.claim: Declining Antarctic sea ice since 2016 means less freshwater during melt season, making the water saltier; ice dropped from a 2014 record high to a record low two years later, and in 2023 was about 1 million square miles below the 1981-2010 average.
insights.speaker: Inside Climate News
insights.so_what: Sea ice loss feeds back into ocean properties.

insights.claim: The layer carries heat, carbon, oxygen and nutrients north into the Indian, Pacific and Atlantic oceans, so changes could alter how the ocean stores and redistributes heat, with impacts possibly within five years.
insights.speaker: Inside Climate News
insights.so_what: Altered ocean heat distribution can affect storms and regional weather.

insights.claim: A scientific review concluded the speed and persistence of sea ice decline suggests the Southern Ocean may be moving into a new state likely to affect the whole global climate system.
insights.speaker: Inside Climate News

insights.claim: Michael Meredith says global climate models used to guide policy still struggle to reflect recent sea-ice losses and 'need to catch up'.
insights.speaker: Inside Climate News
insights.so_what: Policy-relevant climate projections may underestimate change.
insights.quote: Our climate models need to catch up
insights.locator: Paragraph beginning "Meredith said it's not yet clear"

insights.claim: It is not yet clear whether the shift is permanent because the observational record is short, and the Southern Ocean plays a 'massive role' in absorbing human CO2 emissions.
insights.speaker: Inside Climate News
insights.so_what: Disruption to ocean carbon uptake would speed warming.
